claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase microstructure without secondary copper phases.
Processing can produce a fine, uniform 5 vol% copper-nanoparticle dispersion, particularly along grain boundaries.
The copper nanoparticles will reside at grain boundaries or within the high-entropy alloy matrix.
A uniform copper-nanoparticle dispersion will avoid large brittle phases and significant microstructural discontinuities.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Dispersed copper nanoparticles will create rapid heat-transfer pathways through the alloy.
A fine, uniform nanoparticle distribution will minimize stress concentrations.
Minimizing stress concentrations through uniform copper dispersion will inhibit crack initiation and propagation.
Adding approximately 5 vol% copper nanoparticles will significantly increase effective thermal conductivity relative to the undoped alloy.
The copper-doped alloy will maintain mechanical strength under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
The copper-doped alloy will maintain resistance to crack initiation under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
The proposed thermal and mechanical benefits will persist during thermal cycling up to approximately 600°C under loads typical of intermediate plasma-facing reactor components.
Current copper-free intermediate-layer high-entropy alloys have moderate thermal conductivity.
Current copper-free intermediate-layer high-entropy alloys have acceptable but unoptimized structural integrity under reactor conditions.
Copper agglomeration or excessive phase segregation could reduce mechanical strength and negate the intervention's overall benefit.
The expected benefit requires the copper to remain as a stable nanoparticle dispersion under the specified operating conditions.
